U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026
The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced today that the goods and services deficit was $105.0 billion in September, down $0.7 billion from $105.7 billion in August, revised.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, November 4, 2026
Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)
September exports were $321.5 billion, $5.8 billion more than August exports. September imports were $426.6 billion, $5.2 billion more than August imports.
The September decrease in the goods and services deficit reflected a decrease in the goods deficit of $0.7 billion to $135.9 billion and a decrease in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $30.9 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $297.3 billion or 11.6 percent. Imports increased $204.9 billion or 6.2 percent.
Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2)
The average goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the three months ending in September.
Average exports increased $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion in September.
Average imports increased $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion in September.
Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $36.5 billion from the three months ending in September 2025.
Average exports increased $28.9 billion from September 2025.
Average imports increased $65.4 billion from September 2025.

Treatment of Gold in BEA’s International and National Economic Accounts
When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?” and “How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts?”.

Real Goods in 2017 Dollars – Census Basis (exhibit 11)
The real goods deficit increased $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion in September, compared to a 2.2 percent increase in the nominal deficit. (The reason why the Census Basis nominal goods deficit increased, while the BOP nominal goods deficit decreased in September is attributable to a BOP adjustment for nonmonetary gold imports. See “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?”.)
Real exports of goods increased $0.2 billion, or 0.1 percent, to $152.2 billion, compared to a 2.5 percent increase in nominal exports.
Real imports of goods increased $3.6 billion, or 1.4 percent, to $271.6 billion, compared to a 2.4 percent increase in nominal imports.

The September figures show surpluses, in billions of dollars, with Netherlands ($7.7), South and Central America ($6.2), United Kingdom ($3.0), Hong Kong ($2.5), Australia ($2.1), Brazil ($1.1), Singapore ($0.7), Saudi Arabia ($0.5), and Belgium ($0.2). Deficits were recorded, in billions of dollars, with Mexico ($28.7), Vietnam ($25.3), Taiwan ($21.9), China ($17.9), European Union ($14.2), South Korea ($12.2), Germany ($7.9), Italy ($6.3), Malaysia ($5.3), Japan ($4.8), India ($4.5), Canada ($4.4), Ireland ($3.0), Switzerland ($1.3), France ($1.3), and Israel ($0.7).

The deficit with the European Union increased $3.2 billion to $14.2 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.6 billion to $39.0 billion and imports increased $2.6 billion to $53.2 billion.
The deficit with Canada decreased $2.7 billion to $4.4 billion in September. Exports decreased $0.3 billion to $29.7 billion and imports decreased $3.0 billion to $34.1 billion.

Explanatory Notes
Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.
For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.
Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.
Revision procedure (Census basis)
Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau revises the aggregate seasonally adjusted (nominal and real, or chained-dollar) and unadjusted export, import, and trade balance figures, as well as the end-use totals for the prior month. Country detail data and commodity detail data, based on the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC) Revision 4 and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), are not revised monthly. The timing adjustment shown in exhibit 14 is the difference between monthly data as originally reported and as recompiled.
For August 2026, unadjusted exports of goods were revised up $0.1 billion and unadjusted imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion. Goods carry-over in September 2026 was $0.8 billion (0.4 percent) for exports and $0.4 billion (0.1 percent) for imports. For August 2026, revised export carry-over was less than $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent) and revised import carry-over was $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent).
Quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollar series: For March, June, September, and December statistical month releases, revisions are made to the real, or chained-dollar, series presented in exhibits 10 and 11: the previous five months are revised to incorporate the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) revisions to price indexes, which are used to produce the real series and to align Census data with data published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the national income and product accounts (NIPAs).
Annual revisions: Each June, not seasonally adjusted goods data are revised to redistribute monthly data that arrived too late for inclusion in the month of transaction.  BEA 26—45
GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, compared with an increase of 5.0 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent.

Technical Notes
Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

Personal Income and Outlays, September 2026
Personal income increased $54.5 billion (0.2 percent at a monthly rate) in September, according to estimates released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). Personal outlays—the sum of PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments—increased $113.0 billion in September. Personal saving was $911.1 billion, and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of DPI—was 3.8 percent.
The increase in current-dollar personal income in September primarily reflected increases in compensation and government social benefits.
The $113.1 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in September reflected increases of $35.1 billion in spending on goods and $78.1 billion in spending on services.
Real PCE increased $2.6 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in September.
From the preceding month, the PCE price index for September increased 0.5 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.3 percent.
From the same month one year ago, the PCE price index for September increased 3.6 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 3.1 percent from one year ago.

U.S. International Transactions and Investment Position, 2nd Quarter 2026
The U.S. current-account deficit resulting from international economic transactions widened by $33.4 billion, or 15.7 percent, to $246.0 billion in the second quarter of 2026, according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. The revised first-quarter deficit was $212.6 billion.
The second-quarter deficit was 3.0 percent of current-dollar gross domestic product, up from 2.7 percent in the first quarter.
The $33.4 billion widening of the current-account deficit in the second quarter reflected an expanded deficit on goods that was partly offset by reduced deficits on primary (earned) income and on secondary income (current transfers).
Exports of goods and services to, and income received from, foreign residents increased $58.8 billion to $1.44 trillion in the second quarter, reflecting increases in goods exports and in primary (earned) income receipts.
Imports of goods and services from, and income paid to, foreign residents increased $92.2 billion to $1.69 trillion, reflecting increases in goods imports and in primary (earned) income payments.
Capital-transfer receipts decreased $1.1 billion to $2.3 billion in the second quarter. Capital-transfer payments decreased $0.9 billion to $1.0 billion.
Net financial-account transactions were –$369.7 billion in the second quarter, reflecting net U.S. borrowing from foreign residents.1 Second-quarter transactions increased U.S. residents’ foreign financial assets by $663.3 billion and increased U.S. liabilities to foreign residents by $978.9 billion.
The U.S. net international investment position, the difference between U.S. residents’ foreign financial assets and liabilities, was –$22.42 trillion at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Assets totaled $46.97 trillion, and liabilities totaled $69.39 trillion. At the end of the first quarter of 2026, the net investment position was –$21.27 trillion (revised).
U.S. assets increased $3.72 trillion in the second quarter, reflecting increases in all major investment categories except reserve assets. The overall increase was driven by price changes of $3.03 trillion and financial transactions of $663.3 billion.
U.S. liabilities increased $4.87 trillion in the second quarter, reflecting increases in all major investment categories, particularly portfolio investment. The overall increase was driven by price changes of $3.95 trillion and financial transactions of $978.9 billion.

Personal Income and Outlays, July 2026

Real PCE increased $1.3 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in July.

 BEA 26–34
Direct Investment by Country and Industry, 2025
The U.S. direct investment abroad position, or cumulative level of investment, increased $438.1 billion to $7.14 trillion at the end of 2025, according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. The increase was led by a $350.2 billion increase in the position in Europe, primarily in the United Kingdom and Luxembourg. By industry, manufacturing had the largest increase, led by chemical manufacturing.
The foreign direct investment in the United States position increased $266.0 billion to $5.86 trillion at the end of 2025. The increase was led by a $182.4 billion increase in the position from Europe. The largest increase in position was from German multinationals, with a $49.0 billion increase, and the second-largest increase in position was from Canadian multinationals, with a $39.2 billion increase. By industry, manufacturing increased the most, led by electrical equipment and components manufacturing.
U.S. direct investment abroad
U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs) invest in nearly every country, but their investment in affiliates in five countries accounted for more than half of total U.S. direct investment abroad in 2025. The position was largest in the United Kingdom ($1,114.7 billion), followed by the Netherlands ($1,044.0 billion), Luxembourg ($645.3 billion), Ireland ($511.9 billion), and Canada ($488.1 billion).
By industry of the directly owned foreign affiliate, investment was largest in holding companies, which accounted for 45.8 percent of the overall position abroad in 2025. Manufacturing affiliates were second, with 15.9 percent, and finance and insurance affiliates were third, with 13.5 percent, of U.S. investment.
By industry of the U.S. parent, investment by manufacturing MNEs accounted for 50.2 percent of the position, followed by MNEs in finance and insurance (15.8 percent).
U.S. MNEs earned income of $660.1 billion in 2025 on their cumulative investment abroad, an 11.1 percent increase from 2024. Income grew the most in holding companies, increasing $40.0 billion. Income in finance and insurance fell by $6.3 billion compared to 2024.
Foreign direct investment in the United States
By country of the foreign parent, four countries accounted for more than half of total foreign direct investment in the United States in 2025. Japan was the top investing country with a position of $776.3 billion, followed by the Netherlands ($751.8 billion), Canada ($747.3 billion), and the United Kingdom ($738.3 billion).
By country of the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO), the entity at the top of the global ownership chain, Japan was the top investing country in terms of position at the end of 2025, with $827.1 billion. Canada ($819.8 billion) was second, and Germany ($706.2 billion) was third. On the UBO basis, investment from the Netherlands and Luxembourg was much lower than by the country of foreign parent, indicating that much of the investment from foreign parents in these countries was ultimately owned by investors in other countries.
By industry, foreign direct investment in the United States was concentrated in the U.S. manufacturing sector, which accounted for 42.8 percent of the total position. Of the $2.51 trillion foreign investment position in U.S. manufacturing, chemical manufacturing accounted for a third of the total, or $835.9 billion. There was also sizable investment in finance and insurance ($629.7 billion) and wholesale trade ($534.0 billion).
Foreign MNEs earned income of $310.1 billion in 2025 on their cumulative investment in the United States, a 1.9 percent decrease from 2024.

Activities of U.S. Affiliates of Foreign Multinational Enterprises, 2024
Majority-owned U.S. affiliates of foreign multinational enterprises employed 8.57 million workers in the United States in 2024, a 0.2 percent increase from 8.56 million workers in 2023, according to statistics on U.S. affiliate operations and finances released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Research and development (R&D) performed by U.S. affiliates increased 5.3 percent to $95.5 billion. These affiliates accounted for 12.4 percent of total U.S. business R&D in 2024.
 By state, U.S. affiliate employment was highest in California (885,200), Texas (717,400), and New York (556,700). In all three states, U.S. affiliates in the manufacturing sector employed the most workers.

New Foreign Direct Investment in the United States, 2025
Expenditures by foreign direct investors to acquire, establish, or expand U.S. businesses totaled $232.2 billion in 2025, according to preliminary statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. Expenditures increased $76.8 billion, or 49.5 percent, from 2024 levels. As in previous years, acquisitions of existing U.S. businesses accounted for most of the expenditures.
Acquisition expenditures in 2025 were $218.4 billion, expenditures to establish new U.S. businesses were $4.6 billion, and expenditures to expand existing foreign-owned businesses were $9.2 billion. Planned total expenditures, which include both first-year and planned future expenditures, were $284.5 billion.
Employment in 2025 at newly acquired, established, or expanded foreign-owned businesses in the United States was 213,100 employees.
Expenditures by industry, country, and state
By industry, expenditures for new direct investment were largest in publishing industries ($50.7 billion), followed by chemicals manufacturing ($45.4 billion) and plastics and rubber products manufacturing ($19.0 billion). The manufacturing sector ($121.8 billion) accounted for 52.5 percent of total expenditures.
The country with the largest investment was Japan ($50.5 billion), followed by Germany ($26.7 billion) and Canada ($23.5 billion).1 By region, Europe contributed the most new investment, $116.6 billion, or 50.2 percent of all new investment in 2025. Asia and Pacific was the second-largest investing region, with $71.9 billion in expenditures.
By state, California received the most investment in 2025, with $59.7 billion in first-year investment expenditures, followed by Texas ($21.5 billion) and Pennsylvania ($20.9 billion).
Greenfield expenditures
Greenfield investment expenditures—expenditures to establish a new U.S. business or to expand an existing foreign-owned U.S. business—were $13.8 billion in 2025. By industry, greenfield expenditures were largest in transportation and warehousing ($3.6 billion), computers and electronics products manufacturing ($2.0 billion), and chemicals manufacturing ($1.8 billion). By region, investors from Asia and Pacific contributed the highest dollar value of greenfield expenditures ($8.3 billion), led by Australia ($3.0 billion), South Korea ($2.2 billion), and Japan ($1.7 billion). By state, Louisiana ($3.0 billion), Arizona ($2.7 billion), and Texas ($1.9 billion) received the highest levels of greenfield investment.
Planned total expenditures for greenfield investment initiated in 2025, which include both first-year and planned future expenditures, were $66.1 billion.
Employment by industry, country, and state
In 2025, current employment of acquired enterprises was 211,700. Total planned employment, which includes the current employment of acquired enterprises, the planned employment of newly established business enterprises when fully operational, and the planned employment associated with expansions, was 232,400.
By industry, plastics and rubber parts manufacturing accounted for the largest number of current employees (21,800), followed by transportation equipment manufacturing (17,300) and primary and fabricated metals manufacturing (16,400). Mexico (54,600), Canada (29,500), and the United Kingdom (26,800) accounted for the largest number of current employees by country. California (37,200) was the state with the largest current employment resulting from new investment, followed by Illinois (17,600) and Texas (16,500).

Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2024
New Statistics for 2024; Updates for 2020–2023
Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new U.S. data show the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.4 percent ($696.7 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2024 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1).
Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.7 percent in 2024, compared with a 2.8 percent increase for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the increase in outdoor recreation of 5.3 percent in 2023 (national table 1). Real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.0 percent. Outdoor recreation compensation increased 5.2 percent, and employment increased 1.1 percent (national table 9).
Outdoor recreation employment increased in 36 states and the District of Columbia in 2024. The percent change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 4.3 percent in North Dakota to −4.0 percent in Hawaii (BEA interactive tables).
Outdoor recreation by activity
Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures.
In 2024, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.5 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 30.0 percent in 2023. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.0 percent of value added in 2024, compared with 18.8 percent in 2023. Supporting activities accounted for the remaining 51.5 percent of value added in 2024, compared with 51.2 percent in 2023. Growth in supporting activities was led by travel and tourism, reflecting growth in spending on transportation, hotels, and restaurants (national table 4).
Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2024 are as follows (state table 2):
Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $38.4 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 34 states. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.4 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion).
RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $27.5 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in nine states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($5.2 billion), Texas ($2.7 billion), and California ($2.1 billion).
Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $16.5 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($2.0 billion), Florida ($974.6 million), and California ($817.5 million).
Snow activities for the nation was $7.6 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in four states (Colorado, New Hampshire, Utah, and Vermont). The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.6 billion), California ($730.5 million), and Utah ($598.2 million).
Outdoor recreation by industry
The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation.
For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation current-dollar value added in 2024, accounting for $174.4 billion, or 25.0 percent. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 23 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($24.1 billion), Florida ($22.7 billion), and New York ($11.8 billion) (state table 3).
Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $169.1 billion, or 24.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 24 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.3 billion), Texas ($14.4 billion), and Florida ($13.4 billion).
Manufacturing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $91.3 billion, or 13.1 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in two states (Indiana and Louisiana). The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($13.1 billion), California ($11.6 billion), and Indiana ($9.1 billion).
Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics
Estimates for 2020 to 2023 were updated as a part of this release. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation now incorporate the results of the 2025 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts, and newly available and revised source data. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2025 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data.
Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive.

U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela in July were highest since 2017 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
In July 2026, U.S. imports of crude oil from Venezuela averaged 701,000 barrels per day (b/d), the most since May 2017, before decreasing to 655,000 b/d in August, according to data published in our Petroleum Supply Monthly. 
Crude oil imports from Venezuela started the year at 200,000 b/d and have steadily increased most months this year. Increased imports from Venezuela are supported by high crude oil demand from U.S. refineries because of high global refinery margins and the easing of U.S. government restrictions on purchases from the country. Many refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast (PADD 3) are configured to process heavy sour crude oil grades, such as those from Venezuela. 
According to data from Vortexa, the majority of crude oil exports from Venezuela in 2025 were destined for China. In 2026, Venezuela has exported no crude oil to China, and the United States has instead been the largest single destination by volume for Venezuelan crude oil exports. 
U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after the United States imposed sanctions on state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA) in January 2019. In November 2022, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Chevron waivers to resume exporting crude oil from its joint venture operations in Venezuela to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries; Chevron resumed these exports in January 2023. 
The U.S. government eased restrictions on PDVSA following the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and took additional measures to authorize U.S. companies to invest in the country to increase Venezuelan domestic crude oil production.

 November 5, 2026 
Refineries have shifted production away from gasoline to middle distillates 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
Particularly high refinery margins for distillate fuel oil and jet fuel have contributed to shifts in the refinery yields of major products in 2026. Data from our latest Petroleum Supply Monthly—which includes data through August 2026—indicate refinery yields of gasoline have decreased significantly this year to support increased production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, sometimes referred to as middle distillates due to their relative cut points in the oil refining process. 
Petroleum refinery yields represent the share of a specific fuel that is produced from each barrel of crude oil a given refinery (or group of refineries) processes. The U.S. refining fleet tends to have a strong refinery yield of gasoline—typically between 45%–50%. In general terms, for every 100 barrels of crude oil U.S. refiners process, they produce about 45–50 barrels of gasoline. Typically, the most important refinery yields in the United States are the refinery yields of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil (often sold as diesel fuel), and kerosene-type jet fuel. The combined yield of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and jet fuel typically accounts for between 85%–90% of the petroleum products produced by the U.S. refining fleet. 
Despite high gasoline prices, refinery yields of motor gasoline have trended below the five-year (2021–2025) low throughout 2026. This decline largely reflects refinery efforts to shift as much of their yields as possible into the production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, where margins are significantly higher because of constrained global supplies for these fuels. From January through August 2026, refinery yields of gasoline have averaged less than 45% and have been well below the five-year low in every month. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
Conversely, yields of distillate fuel oil have generally been higher than last year and have been above the five-year average in every month. Even more than for gasoline, crack spreads and refinery margins for distillate fuel have been elevated for most of this year in response to limits on global supplies of the fuel. 
Refinery yields of jet fuel have also been relatively high this year. The U.S. refinery fleet exceeded an average jet fuel yield of 12% for the first time in March 2026, according to EIA data. Since then, the fleetwide average jet fuel yield has remained at or above 12% through the latest Petroleum Supply Monthly data for August 2026. Jet fuel yields were already setting the five-year high for most of 2025; elevated jet fuel margins in 2026 have provided a persistent incentive for refiners to continue maximizing jet fuel production. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly

 November 3, 2026 
Global refinery inputs fell sharply in the second quarter of 2026 before modest recovery 
Data source: Kpler
Note: 2Q2025=second quarter of 2025 
Global crude oil refinery inputs fell by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), or 6%, following the start of conflict in late February in the Middle East, according to data from Kpler. Throughput then increased by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter, primarily as refiners in the region adjusted to new trade flows. 
Crude oil inputs to refineries typically increase in the second and third quarters of the year as refiners complete planned maintenance and gear up to meet peak seasonal demand for refined products, such as gasoline and jet fuel. Global crude oil inputs increased by 0.3 million b/d in the second quarter of 2025 and by another 2 million b/d in the third quarter. 
The countries with the largest refining capacity in the world are the United States, China, Russia, and India. Refining in countries most directly impacted by the loss of crude oil supply from conflict in the Strait of Hormuz saw the largest declines. Crude oil refinery inputs in China fell by 2.1 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26, while crude oil inputs in India, South Korea, and Japan fell by more than 1.0 million b/d collectively in 2Q26 before rebounding by 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. 
Crude oil inputs also fell in the Middle East as the closure of the strait significantly limited the export of refined products. Crude oil inputs fell by 0.7 million b/d in Kuwait, 0.7 million b/d in the United Arab Emirates, 0.3 million b/d in Saudi Arabia, and 0.2 million b/d in Iran in 2Q26. Total crude oil inputs in these four countries increased by 0.4 million b/d in 3Q26. 
Increased attacks on Russian oil infrastructure during the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine reduced refinery crude oil inputs in Russia by 0.6 million b/d in 2Q26 and an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. Russia is a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel fuel, so the decline in exports affected global diesel markets that were already tight from earlier geopolitical developments. This loss in refinery operations compounded reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September. 
Although crude oil inputs were falling in some countries in the second and third quarters of 2026, they increased in the United States and in some other regions that were able to find alternative sources of supply. Crude oil refinery inputs in the United States increased by 0.5 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.5 million b/d in 3Q26, as the United States increasingly exported refined products around the world to make up for lost supply. 
Global refinery crude oil inputs recovered somewhat in 3Q26, increasing by 1.8 million b/d overall as increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz, alternative routes, and ship-to-ship transfers put more Middle Eastern crude oil on the global market. Despite the increase in oil flows and refinery inputs, crude oil inputs in 3Q26 still remained about 5% lower on average than during the same period of 2025.

The share of solar generation with co-located battery storage is increasing 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report 
Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators. 
Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. 
When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment. 
We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. 
Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

 October 29, 2026 
LNG imports make up increasing share of Colombia’s natural gas supply 
 Data source: Gestor del Mercado de Gas Natural en Colombia (BEC), Bolsa Mercantil de Colombia (BMC) 
Colombia is importing more liquefied natural gas (LNG) as domestic production continues to fall. A potential drought this fall and winter could limit the availability of hydroelectric generation and boost the country’s demand for natural gas power generation. Colombia’s government has declared a national disaster in anticipation of a drought resulting from an expected strong El Niño. 
Average annual marketed natural gas production in Colombia decreased from 1,070 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) in 2022 to 772 MMcf/d in 2025, according to Gestor del Mercado de Gas Natural en Columbia (BEC). Between January and August 2026, production declined further, averaging 673 MMcf/d. The fields that produce most of Colombia’s natural gas—specifically Cusiana, Cupiagua, Pauto Sur, and the offshore Guajira fields—have been declining since 2022, with no large discoveries developed to replace them. Proved reserves fell 39% to 1.7 trillion cubic feet between 2022 and 2025, according to the National Hydrocarbons Agency. 
As production declined, LNG imports grew. LNG imports accounted for a record 31% of Colombia’s monthly natural gas supply in July 2026, according to data from BEC, Colombia’s gas market administrator. 
Despite the increased reliance on imports, Colombia only has one operating LNG import terminal, SPEC LNG, which is located near Cartagena on the Caribbean coast. Work is under way to expand the terminal’s capacity to be online in 2026 and as early as end of October, according to Promigas. A new project, the Buenaventura LNG terminal, is targeting to startup by November 2026. In addition, the Puerto Bahia LNG Terminal and Ballenas LNG Terminal could start operations next year. 
On June 11, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced that an El Niño formed in the tropical Pacific. In October 2026, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño Advisory, reporting that the El Niño continues to strengthen and that there’s a greater than 83% chance of a strong to very-strong event through the first quarter of 2027. NOAA considers an El Niño event to be strong when ocean temperatures in the Niño-monitored region of the Pacific Ocean are equal to or exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius, and a very strong event occurs when ocean temperatures equal or exceed 2.0 degrees Celsius. 
 Data source: Electricity production by fuel source, Colombia Ministry of Energy, Mining and Energy Planning Unit (UPME) 
El Niño typically brings drier-than-normal weather to northern South America from December through February, according to NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, reducing the availability of hydropower. Natural gas consumption in Colombia’s electric power sector spiked in 2023 and 2024 when there was a strong El Niño weather pattern. In 2025, hydropower supplied 81% of the country’s electricity, natural gas supplied 8%, and coal supplied 4%. By comparison, hydropower made up 55% of the country’s electricity in March 2024, the last strong El Niño year, while natural gas-fired generation rose to 22% and coal-fired generation rose to 15%. 
The share of hydropower electricity generation fell to 66% in July 2026 while coal and natural gas each accounted for 12% of electricity generation. If a strong El Niño persists, natural gas will likely play a larger role in electricity generation.

 October 22, 2026 
U.S. refineries have been running at very high rates in 2026 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Petroleum Status Report 
The U.S. refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilization averaging more than 95% of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998. Tight global product supplies this year have boosted margins for petroleum products, particularly for diesel, incentivizing the increased run rates. 
Since 1991, U.S. refinery utilization has averaged 92% from May to September, compared with 88% across the other seven months. 
U.S. refineries tend to run at their highest rates between May and September to boost supply of gasoline for the peak demand season in the summer months. Distillate demand, by contrast, peaks in the fall and winter. Because refineries produce a combination of gasoline and distillates, high summer refinery utilization usually leads to an increase in distillate inventories before seasonal refinery maintenance and the peak distillate demand season. 
This year the refinery runs were driven largely by tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for U.S. distillate fuel oil exports. 
While refinery utilization was the highest since 1998, total U.S. refinery output was only the highest since 2019 because refining capacity has decreased by 4% since then. 
In the first 3 weeks of October, U.S. refinery utilization decreased from its summer highs but remained above the five-year (2021–2025) seasonal average.

 October 19, 2026 
Hybrid sales rise while battery electric sales remain lower after tax credit expiration 
 Data source: Omdia 
 Note: 1Q16=first quarter 2016; 3Q26=third quarter 2026 
In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% in 3Q25. Between 3Q25 and 3Q26, hybrid electric vehicles continued to gain market share, reaching 16% of light-duty vehicle sales. Growth of hybrid electric vehicle sales has slowed this quarter as the average transaction price for a new vehicle passed $50,000—the first time this price has been reached so far this year, according to Kelley Blue Book. 
The market shares of battery electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles decreased over the same period, according to estimates from Omdia. In 3Q26, battery electric vehicle sales were 6% of new light-duty vehicles sold, down from 10% in 3Q25; plug-in hybrid electric vehicle sales fell from 1.8% to 0.7% over the same period. 
These vehicle types affect the broader energy sector in different ways. Battery electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles consume electricity from the grid, which affects electricity demand. By comparison, hybrid electric vehicles consume liquid fuels and do not connect to the grid. Hybrid vehicles were not eligible for any of the federal tax credits that expired in September 2025. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Types of Electric Vehicles 
Two tax credits for purchasing or leasing new electric vehicles expired on September 30, 2025: the New Clean Vehicle Credit and the Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit. Battery electric vehicles made up a record 12% of light-duty vehicle sales in September 2025, immediately before the credits expired. However, 2025 marked the first year where annual sales and market share of battery electric vehicles declined, a trend that has continued in 2026. Battery electric vehicle sales fell to 6% of new vehicle sales in the first nine months of 2026, down from 8% over the same period in 2025. 
Battery electric vehicles have historically been more popular in the U.S. luxury vehicle segment, which accounted for 12% of the total U.S. light-duty vehicle sales in 3Q26. However, sales in this segment are also declining. In 3Q26, battery electric vehicles accounted for 12% of luxury light-duty vehicle sales, down from 31% in 3Q25 prior to the expiration of the clean vehicle tax credits. 
 Data source: Omdia 
Because sales figures in any year are relatively small compared with the total number of vehicles on the road, electric vehicles’ share of the light-duty vehicle fleet is much less than the recent total 6% sales share in 3Q26. In 2024, the most recent year for which we have fleet-wide data available in our Monthly Energy Review, electric vehicles accounted for 2% of all registered light-duty vehicles in the United States.

 October 16, 2026 
U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Annual Electric Power Industry Report 
We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country—California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida—are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives. 
The year-over-year change in generation was particularly high in 2022, when total generation grew by 25% compared with the previous year amid record capacity growth. Changes in different programs supporting rooftop solar partly explain this increase in generation. For example, California’s Net Energy Metering (NEM) 2.0 program was available through April 2023. This net metering program offered higher export compensation than the subsequent Net Billing Tariff, or NEM 3.0. All the capacity built under the NEM 2.0 program was grandfathered in, incentivizing higher capacity installation before the current NEM 3.0 took effect. 
California accounted for 37% (34,411 GWh) of total U.S. small-scale solar generation in 2025. Between 2024 and 2025, rooftop solar generation in the state grew by 8%, largely due to an increase in capacity. Small-scale solar capacity in California increased from 18 gigawatts in 2024 to 20 gigawatts in 2025. 
The state with the next largest amount of small-scale solar power generation is Arizona, accounting for over 6% of total U.S. generation, or 5,795 GWh. Year-over-year generation in Arizona grew only 6% in 2025. The largest increase happened between 2022 and 2023 when generation from small-scale solar grew by 22% in the state. Arizona customers can access a 25% state income-tax credit and other incentives for adding rooftop solar to their properties. 
States such as Florida and Texas have seen rapid growth in small-scale solar generation in the last decade as more capacity has been added. Generation in Texas grew from 391 GWh in 2016 to 5,408 GWh last year. Over the same period, Florida’s generation grew from 205 GWh in 2016 to 5,198 GWh in 2025. These two states provide incentives through property tax exemptions and other programs specific to each state and, in some cases, utility. 
Programs in states with lower irradiance levels are also supporting growth in rooftop solar generation. New York offers incentives, which have encouraged small-scale solar growth in the state. Other states with similar programs include New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Illinois. 
Although generation from small-scale solar continues to grow year over year, the rate of growth has declined since 2022. 
EIA uses its surveys of electric utilities to collect information on the number of customers with small-scale solar systems and the aggregated capacity. Electric utilities do not necessarily know how much electricity is generated by rooftop solar on their distribution systems, so generation must be estimated. To develop estimates of generation, we rely on tools such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisor Model and PVWatts. Data on commonly used tilt angles and orientations for small-scale solar systems in California were used as inputs to be representative of tilt angles and orientations in other states.

PJM, ERCOT, and SWPP all set peak load records this summer 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Hourly Electric Grid Monitor 
 Note: Data are the highest hourly load for a given day. ISO=independent system operator, ERCOT=Electric Reliability Council of Texas, SWPP=Southwest Power Pool 
Three regional transmission organizations (RTOs) set records for peak hourly load this past summer, according to data reported on Form EIA-930 and presented in the Hourly Electric Grid Monitor: 
PJM peaked at 162.6 gigawatts (GW) on July 2, 2026, 1.3% higher than the pre-2026 peak of 160.6 GW on June 23, 2025. 
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) peaked at 91.1 GW on July 22, 2026, 6.5% higher than the pre-2026 record of 85.5 GW on August 20, 2024. 
The Southwest Power Pool (SWPP) peaked at 58.0 GW on July 27, 2026, 3.5% higher than the pre-2026 peak of 56.0 GW on August 21, 2023. 
Most of these peaks occurred during regional heat waves, amid the hottest summer on record nationally, which drove up cooling demand. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Hourly Electric Grid Monitor 
 Note: : ISO=independent system operator, MISO=Midcontinent Independent System Operator, CAISO=California Independent System Operator, NYISO=New York Independent System Operator, and ISO-NE=Independent System Operator New England 
The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) and the Independent System Operator for New England (ISO-NE) came within 2% of their previous records. The New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) was within 3% of its previous record load, and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) was within 4%, according to Form EIA-930: 
CAISO reached 50.0 GW on September 9, 2026, below its record high of 51.1 GW reached on September 6, 2022. 
ISO-NE reached 25.3 GW on July 2, 2026, below its record of 25.9 GW on June 24, 2025. 
NYISO reached 31.1 GW on July 2, 2026, below its previous record of 31.9 GW on June 24, 2025 (NYISO reports a record of 34.0 GW set in 2013, before we collected hourly data). 
MISO peaked at 121.5 gigawatts (GW) on June 30, 2026, the highest in our Hourly Electric Grid Monitor but below the previous peak of 127.1 GW on July 20, 2011, as reported by MISO. 
Data from Form EIA-930 is reported to us by each balancing authority (BA) and is made available "as-is". The data BAs report on the Form EIA-930 represent best values at the time of reporting, but various reporting issues may limit the quality of these data. Data published directly by BAs may differ from the data in Form EIA-930.

Monthly wind generation in the first nine months of 2026 was an average of 68% higher compared with the same period in 2025 in ISO New England (ISO-NE): 
Monthly generation from wind was highest in September of this year at 668.9 gigawatthours (GWh), more than double generation levels from September 2025 and nearly 10% higher than this year’s previous high in March.

 October 9, 2026 
Hurricane Isaias nears landfall, leading to production shut-ins 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, U.S. Energy Atlas map of hurricanes, cyclones, and typhoons; National Weather Service’s National Hurricane Center
Note: LNG=liquefied natural gas 
As of 4:00 a.m. central time on October 9, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects Hurricane Isaias to make landfall on the Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, creating the potential for significant disruptions to energy infrastructure. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. 
Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations.

 October 7, 2026 
Mixed outlook for energy expenditures this winter 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook 
We expect energy expenditures this winter to vary because of diverging trends in energy prices among fuels and regional variation in forecast temperatures. We expect that lower prices for natural gas and propane will drive decreases in expenditures this year for the half of U.S. households heating with those fuels. Higher prices for electricity and heating oil drive increased expenditures for households heating with those fuels in our forecast. 
Although we expect national average temperatures to be similar to last winter, our forecast assumes warmer temperatures in the Northeast, following a relatively cold winter last year, and much colder temperatures in the West, following an unusually warm winter last year. Temperatures in the Midwest and South are similar to last year. 
Homes that use heating oil as their main heating fuel—about 3% of U.S. homes, which are mostly in the Northeast—could see the largest increase in spending this year. We expect a 21% increase in spending on heating oil compared with last winter, driven by increasing global distillate prices. We forecast the price of heating oil will average 34% more this winter than last winter, but warmer forecast temperatures are expected to partly offset our forecast increase in prices. We expect the more than 40% of homes heating with electricity will experience a 4% increase in electricity bills on average. We expect energy expenditures will decrease on average by 9% in homes heating with natural gas and by 3% in those heating with propane. 
Distillate dynamics 
Global distillate fuel production, which includes heating oil production, has dropped because of reduced global refining activity. Lower production has caused rising international prices, driving up both the cost to import distillate to the United States and the demand for distillate exports from the United States. Through the first seven months of 2026, U.S. distillate exports increased 20% over the same period last year, with much of the increased volumes sent to Europe. 
With more costly U.S. imports and higher demand for U.S. exports, U.S. distillate fuel stocks are low heading into winter. We expect inventories will be about 11% below the five-year average in the fourth quarter of 2026. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook

 October 5, 2026 
Crude oil prices and refinery margins generally increased throughout the third quarter 
 Data source: Bloomberg L.P. 
 Note: 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 
Petroleum markets in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26) were characterized by increasing prices for crude oil and petroleum products amid persistent conflict in the Middle East. 
Crude oil prices
Crude oil prices steadily climbed in 3Q26 as markets adjusted to renewed military strikes in the Middle East. The front-month futures price of a barrel of Brent crude oil began the quarter at $72 per barrel (b) on July 1, the lowest since February 26, two days before the start of the war. The low prices at the start of the quarter reflected increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz in June following the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). 
Following the resumption of military strikes on July 7, crude oil prices increased, with the futures price passing $100/b on July 23 and then trading between $79/b and $98/b until September 8. Daily price volatility in this period generally reflected: 
Market responses to public statements by U.S., Iranian, and other regional leaders on military plans and the likelihood of a peace deal 
Flows and disruptions to flows through the Strait of Hormuz 
Other supply risks and disruptions, such as attacks on oil export infrastructure in Russia 
Crude oil futures prices passed $100/b again on September 9 following an escalation of military action against energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia, including: 
U.S. and Iranian attacks on crude oil tankers 
U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports 
Attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline 
Attacks on Saudi Arabian oil tankers around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait 
Ukraine’s drone attacks on Novorossiysk, one of Russia’s major oil terminals on the Black Sea 
Prices also increased because some of the measures that had helped to mitigate the price effects of reduced global supplies earlier in the year began to unwind. Since April, reduced crude oil imports to China lowered global oil demand, absorbing some of the shock of reduced supply from the Middle East. In 3Q26, China continued to import far less crude oil than it did before the war. However, China’s 3Q26 crude oil imports were up from May and June, adding some demand back into the market. Additionally, releases from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve slowed significantly in September, limiting additional sources of supply as the disruption has continued. 
The futures price for Brent crude oil peaked on September 15 at $109/b while spot prices reached as high as $132/b around the same time. Like in April, disruptions of supply—particularly out of Saudi Arabia—put more pressure on Brent crude oil spot prices as buyers struggled to find short-term supply amid the escalating military action. Crude oil prices averaged around $104/b in the final two weeks of the quarter as markets balanced peace discussions with the possibility of a wider scale war. 
Refinery margins
Like in the previous quarter, U.S. refineries ran at unseasonally high levels in 3Q26 with utilization averaging 95%, processing the most crude oil for the third quarter since 2019, when refining capacity was 4% higher. High refinery inputs reflected strong margins for transportation fuels. Motor gasoline, distillate, and jet fuel crack spreads—measures of the refinery margins for these fuels—were all elevated. The quarterly average gasoline crack spread more than doubled the year-ago level despite declining in the second half of the quarter, and the distillate and jet fuel crack spreads almost tripled their year-ago levels as a result of tight global supply. 
 Data source: Bloomberg L.P. 
 Note: The crack spreads reflect the New York Harbor spot prices for RBOB, ultra-low sulfur diesel, and jet fuel minus the Dated Brent spot price. 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 
Crack spreads were highest for distillate fuel oil and second highest for jet fuel because the disrupted refining activities in Russia, China, and the Middle East supplied large shares of these fuels to global markets. U.S. distillate fuel supplies have become tight because of high exports to markets in short supply, as well as higher costs for importing regions, such as the U.S. East Coast. As of the week ending September 25, U.S. distillate fuel inventories were 13% below the five-year (2021–2025) average while U.S. gasoline inventories and jet fuel inventories were 7% below and 3% above their five-year averages, respectively.

 October 2, 2026 
U.S. natural gas production reached a record high in July 2026 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Natural Gas Monthly 
U.S. natural gas production hit an all-time high in July 2026, driven primarily by increased output in the Permian Basin, according to our latest Natural Gas Monthly. 
Gross withdrawals—the total volume of gas extracted at the wellhead—reached a record 137 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) in July 2026. It was the first new monthly record for gross withdrawals in 2026, following five record-setting months in 2025. 
The July 2026 record was driven primarily by new wells coming online in Texas and New Mexico. The Permian region, which includes parts of western Texas and eastern New Mexico, is one of the most prolific oil and gas regions in the world and has been experiencing increased gas-to-oil ratios. U.S. natural gas production grew in 2025 as a result of higher natural gas prices, continued gains in new well productivity, and increased operational efficiency. 
Gross withdrawals in Texas and New Mexico increased by a combined 1.7 Bcf/d (3.2%) from June to July 2026. Gross withdrawals were also up in Louisiana, Oklahoma, and North Dakota in July 2026, each by more than 0.1 Bcf/d. 
New natural gas pipeline infrastructure is easing long-standing gas transport bottlenecks in Texas. One of these projects, the Hugh Brinson Pipeline, began interstate pipeline flows ahead of schedule this summer. New pipelines increase the takeaway capacity out of the Permian Basin to liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminals on the Gulf Coast, supporting production growth. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Natural Gas Monthly 
We publish three different estimates of natural gas production: 
Gross withdrawals reflect the full well stream volume of natural gas from both oil and gas wells. 
Marketed production is gross withdrawals less gas used for repressuring, vented and flared gas, and nonhydrocarbon gases removed. 
Dry production reflects consumer-grade natural gas and excludes natural gas plant liquids. 
July 2026 also set all-time records for marketed production and dry gas production.

U.S. exports of propane reached records in the first half of 2026 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
U.S. propane exports increased to 2 million barrels per day (b/d) in the first half of 2026, 11% more than during the same period in 2025. Increased U.S. propane production and changing trade flows, particularly increased exports to India and other countries in South Asia, drove propane exports to a record high of 2.1 million b/d in April 2026. Since then, total propane exports, including exports to India, have continued at levels well above the five-year average. 
Record U.S. propane production has supported the rise in propane exports. Propane production, which is a byproduct of natural gas processing and crude oil refining, has increased rapidly over the past 10 years as U.S. natural gas output has grown. Higher propane production has led to lower U.S. propane prices relative to Asia, underpinning the record export levels. 
Propane is consumed globally in the residential and commercial sectors for space heating and other uses. It’s also used as a petrochemical feedstock to produce propylene and ethylene, key feedstocks in plastic production. 
U.S. propane exports surpassed 2 million b/d in April 2026 for the first time, driven by increased demand for petrochemicals and for importers seeking supplies to replace disrupted shipments from the Middle East. Favorable prices for U.S. propane exports also outpaced competition in other regions. An expansion project by Enterprise, expected to be completed this year at the Houston Ship Channel and Nederland terminals, will increase capacity by another 300,000 b/d. 
While U.S. exports for propane have increased, trade flows have changed. In February 2025, China imposed a 10% tariff on propane imports from the United States, which decreased demand for U.S. exports of propane. China’s tariffs on U.S. propane rose to 125% for the month of April 2025 before falling and remaining at 10% since May 2025. U.S. exports of propane to China were down 28% in 2025, compared with 2024. In the first half of 2026, U.S. propane exports to China fell by 19% compared with January to June 2025. 
Continued growth in propane exports could be constrained by export capacity limitations. In addition to these capacity limitations, ongoing drought conditions at the Panama Canal related to the El Niño weather effect are also curtailing current propane exports. Low water levels at the Panama Canal limit the number of ships that can transit the canal daily and increase the effective costs associated with the canal’s use. For propane exports that pass through the canal, these costs must be absorbed by buyers and sellers and could hinder U.S. propane exports.

Member of the ECB's Executive Board 
SPEECH
The science and practice of monetary policy communication: the ECB experience
Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Bank of England and its Watchers Conference
London, 10 November 2026
Monetary policy is about more than just the latest interest rate decision. It also involves communication about future economic developments and the factors shaping future policy decisions.[1] By steering the expectations of financial market participants, central bank communication shapes the full set of financial market prices across the maturity and risk spectrums, in turn affecting financing conditions and decisions around credit, saving and investment. The decisions of households and firms are also affected by their beliefs about monetary policy, which depend on how the central bank communicates.[2] 
I will divide this speech into two parts. In the first part, I will review recent contributions by ECB staff on the science of monetary policy communication.[3] In the second part, I will discuss the practice of monetary policy communication from an ECB perspective.
The science of monetary policy communication 
Greater data availability, increased computing power and artificial intelligence have substantially expanded the tools available for analysing central bank communication. Until recently, researchers relied on dictionary-based approaches to quantify the content and tone of monetary policy statements and speeches. This involved categorising specific words and expressions associated with a restrictive or accommodative stance, or with different assessments of inflation and the economic outlook.[4] Machine learning techniques and large language models (LLMs) now allow for the extensive analysis of large volumes of text in a more automated manner, taking into account the context in which words are used instead of relying solely on the frequency of individual words or predefined expressions.[5]
Recent ECB research illustrates these possibilities. A set of novel, LLM-based in-house measures of the tone of ECB monetary policy communication confirms that it becomes more hawkish during tightening phases and more dovish during easing periods. These shifts in communication closely track developments in the deposit facility rate (Chart 1, panel a).[6] The importance of communication is also illustrated by the research finding that information extracted from ECB monetary policy statements can improve forecasts of euro area core inflation several quarters ahead, even when controlling for the contributions of Eurosystem and ECB staff projections.[7]
These indicators can also be employed to test whether central bank communication follows systematic patterns that reflect the economic outlook and the policy stance. Indeed, the evidence suggests that central banks tend to communicate in a systematic manner, following “communication rules”.[8] By estimating a systematic relationship between the tone of communication on monetary policy, economic activity and inflation, ECB staff find that, in line with our primary objective of price stability, ECB communication on monetary policy systematically places more emphasis on inflation developments (Chart 1, panel b).
These new tools therefore provide valuable insights into aspects of communication that conventional financial market indicators may not fully capture. At the same time, their use requires careful validation, since the results depend on how questions are formulated and what data are used for training.[9] 
Chart 1
Evolution of ECB communication tone and “Taylor-type” communication rule weights

a) LLM-based sentiment scores and the deposit facility rate (DFR) | 
b) estimated communication rules linking tone on monetary policy with tone on inflation and economic activity

Notes: Panel a): sentiment scores across three communication dimensions (left-hand scale) and the DFR (right-hand scale). “Monetary policy” captures the tone of communication surrounding policy decisions, “economic activity” reflects assessments of economic developments and “inflation” captures signals related to price developments. A score of zero indicates a neutral tone, while positive and negative values indicate hawkish and dovish tones, respectively. Sentiment scores are calculated as moving averages of the scores for the most recent 30 texts. The sample period is 14 January 2001 to 26 October 2026. 
Panel b): regression coefficients for a model regressing the de-meaned values of the monetary policy tone on the de-meaned inflation and economic activity tones, using the tone as measured at the ECB Governing Council meeting, with the inflation and economic weights constrained to sum to one. Whiskers show 95% heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation-consistent confidence intervals. The sample period is 1 January 2001 to 13 August 2026.
Financial markets 
Financial market participants closely follow central bank communication because it provides information about both the economic and inflation outlook and the expected path of monetary policy. Both of these dimensions are relevant for asset pricing and investment decisions.
Central bank communication can influence interest rate expectations and financial conditions, independently from actual policy changes.[10] Research shows that financial analysts reassess the monetary policy stance following ECB Governing Council announcements, considering both the policy decision and the accompanying communication. Unexpected revisions in their assessment contain information beyond conventional market-based monetary policy surprises and are associated with significant effects on economic and financial conditions. For instance, even when an interest rate decision is widely anticipated and generates little immediate market reaction, the accompanying communication may lead market analysts to reassess how restrictive is monetary policy or how it is likely to evolve.[11] 
Chart 2
Communication moves financial markets
Cumulated absolute high-frequency changes in risk-free rates by event type
(basis points)
Source: Akkaya, Y., Bitter, L., Grasso, A. and Amorim Cabaco, B. (2025), “From press conferences to speeches: the impact of the ECB’s monetary policy communication”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 1, ECB.
Notes: Cumulated absolute high-frequency changes (with mean absolute changes in brackets) for a range of risk-free and sovereign yields across event types, computed using data from January 2004 to October 2023. The high-frequency window around the different event types is as follows: -10 minutes to +20 minutes around publication of the monetary policy press release; -10 minutes to +75 minutes around the start of the Governing Council’s press conference; -10 minutes to +50 minutes around the publication of the account of the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting; -10 minutes to +80 minutes around the publication of the Monthly/Economic Bulletin; -10 minutes to +60 minutes around the publication of speeches other than statements to the European Parliament; and -10 minutes to +10 minutes around the publication of Bloomberg headlines. “OIS” stands for overnight index swap.
The importance of communication extends beyond Governing Council meetings. Research examining thousands of speeches, interviews, hearings and other events shows that communication in the time period between meetings can affect market interest rates across maturities. It can help markets anticipate policy changes, particularly ahead of tightening episodes, and its cumulative effect over time can be comparable to that of policy announcements, especially at longer maturities (Chart 2).[12]
Beyond shaping expectations about the future path of policy rates, communication also affects financial conditions more broadly. The tone of ECB communication can influence monetary policy uncertainty and premia on risky assets.[13] In particular, financial markets respond to several dimensions of monetary policy news: the current policy rate, the expected path of rates, and market and sovereign risk (“target”, “path”, and “risk” in Chart 3, respectively).

Monetary policy news from selected ECB Governing Council meetings
(standard deviations)
Sources: Bloomberg and ECB calculations.
Notes: The model decomposes movements in overnight index swaps (one, three and six months; one, two, five and ten years), ten-year sovereign yields (DE, FR, IT and ES), a set of risky assets (Eurostoxx 50, Eurostoxx Banks, Eurostoxx VSTOXX) and the EUR/USD exchange rate into three factors: interest rate target, path and risk. Average interest rate uncertainty is based on the option-implied standard deviation of the three-month Euribor one year ahead. The latest observations are for 29 October 2026.
Households and firms
Communicating with households and firms presents different challenges to communicating with markets. Unlike professional market participants, most households do not closely follow central bank communication. And even when they do encounter central bank messages, they may interpret their implications differently to market analysts. Research presented in our 2021 monetary policy strategy review suggests that information about the new inflation target reached only around one in ten consumers in the months following its announcement. Most learned about the new inflation target through television, radio and newspapers rather than directly from the ECB (Chart 4).[14]
Chart 4
How ECB communication reaches households
Consumer Expectations Survey responses on channels for information about ECB 
(percentage shares of all respondents)
Source: Ehrmann, M., Georgarakos, D. and Kenny, G. (2025), “Credibility gains from central bank communication with the public”, European Economic Review, Vol. 177, No 105069.
Notes: Responses to the question “In the past two months, have you seen or heard information about the European Central Bank (ECB) from any of the following sources?”. The figure reports the percentage share of all respondents, by answer category. Apart from “No info”, all other options are not mutually exclusive, leading to a total sum higher than 100 per cent of the respondents. Weighted estimates. The last observation is for August 2026 (most recent Consumer Expectations Survey).
Reaching households, however, is just one part of the process. Attention to inflation varies with the economic environment. When inflation is high, households and firms tend to pay more attention, while they pay less attention when inflation is low and stable (Chart 5).[15] This matters for the transmission of monetary policy. What households and firms believe about future inflation, and how confident they are that the central bank will deliver price stability, shapes how they set wages and prices and how they adjust their spending and saving when we change interest rates.[16] 
When inflation is high, households tend to be more attentive, but they may also be less responsive to information they already know. This underscores the importance of tailoring communication to the economic environment to ensure that messages reach households when inflation is low while providing clear, relevant and informative explanations when inflation becomes more salient.[17]
