SPEECH 
Cash and the digital euro: two sides of the same coin
Introductory statement by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs of the European Parliament
Brussels, 10 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back here for the first time since the Parliament adopted its position on the Single Currency Package, and I very much welcome the broad support it received in the plenary session on 9 July. This gives a strong democratic backing to the digital euro. Let me also thank you for the considerable work and constructive dialogue that have made this progress possible.
A swift conclusion of the ongoing trilogue negotiations would pave the way for the adoption of the Single Currency Package[1] by the end of the year as foreseen in the One Europe, One Market Roadmap.[2] This would give us the legal certainty needed to complete our preparations for the digital euro. It would also give certainty to the market regarding the planned date for a possible first issuance, which can be set only after the Regulation is adopted. A delay in adoption could instead postpone the introduction of the digital euro, further entrench Europe’s dependence on foreign providers, and make it more difficult for European companies to innovate and compete.
Europe’s achievements in payments innovation go beyond progress on the digital euro. In September we launched Pontes, which connects market distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms with the Eurosystem’s TARGET Services.[3] The launch was widely welcomed by the market, with 18 market participants and market DLT operators onboarded on day one and many others preparing to join soon. Pontes makes the settlement of tokenised transactions in central bank money an operational reality and is a major milestone in the development of digital European capital markets. On 2 November it settled the issuance of the European Stability Mechanism’s first digitally native benchmark bond of €1 billion[4], facilitating the shift in European tokenised finance from experimentation to adoption.
While I am happy to answer any questions on Pontes, I would like to focus my remarks today on the digital euro and cash.
Preparing for the digital euro pilot and first issuance 
We are moving ahead with preparations for the digital euro pilot. It will test the digital euro’s technical functionality, operational processes and user experience, using a beta version without legal tender status. 
Starting in the second half of 2027, the pilot will involve Eurosystem staff, participating payment service providers (PSPs) and selected merchants offering everyday services – for example in canteens – at the ECB and participating national central banks.
We have seen strong market interest in the pilot and, in July, we announced the 36 PSPs selected to join the pilot from more than 50 applicants.[5] They include banks and non-bank providers, and cover a broad range of business models, sizes and geographical locations.
We are working closely with participating PSPs to hear their views and benefit from their experience.[6] 
In September we opened an additional call for online and mobile merchants to join the pilot to test remote payments. The final selection of merchants will be announced early next year.[7] 
This collaboration with market players is essential. The digital euro must work on a technical level, but also in everyday life – for consumers, merchants and PSPs.
Looking further ahead, we are planning for the digital euro rollout. 
On our side, we plan to ensure that all relevant use cases[8] for the digital euro are made technically available from first issuance. At the same time, feedback from market participants[9] shows that a gradual rollout would support a smooth and successful first issuance by giving them sufficient time to adapt. We are glad that the co-legislators intend to provide legal clarity on the feasibility of such a phased rollout in shops. 
In preparation for first issuance, we are also working more closely with the market on the digital euro innovation platform. 
In September we launched a new call for expression of interest, inviting private companies and organisations to explore how the digital euro can foster market innovation.[10] The next wave of activities, including testing conditional payments and exploring applications of artificial intelligence in payments, will run from January to June 2027.[11]
Redesigning euro banknotes 
Innovation also extends to banknotes. In July we invited Europeans to share their views on ten shortlisted design proposals for the new euro banknotes based on the themes “European culture” and “Rivers and birds”. 
The survey received almost 10 million responses, with high participation across all euro area countries and age groups.[12] This demonstrates how deeply Europeans care about their money.
The survey results will inform the ECB Governing Council’s decision on the final design concept, expected around the end of this year. At that point, we will also publish the survey results. First denominations of the new banknote series are expected to enter into circulation in the early 2030s.[13]
But cash must also remain widely available and accepted in practice. We therefore support strong legislative provisions on mandatory cash acceptance, access to cash across the euro area and the resilience of cash infrastructure.
Conclusion 
Let me conclude.
In today’s uncertain geopolitical environment, timely progress on the digital euro is essential to strengthen Europe’s autonomy in payments. We are doing our part by progressing with the technical preparations. But the adoption of the legal framework is necessary to finalise the digital euro’s design and Rulebook[14] and, ultimately, to issue the digital euro.
In two months’ time we will mark the 25th anniversary of euro banknotes and coins entering circulation. While cash is still widely used in shops, digital payments are growing. I therefore hope that by then we will have a strong legal framework in place: one that both safeguards the acceptance of cash and gives Europeans a digital form of cash alongside it.
Thank you.

and AST SpaceMobile Establish “Rakuten AST” Joint
Venture to Build D2D Satellite Communications Network in Japan
-
Approximately USD 1 billion in funding awarded from Japan’s MIC to support deployment of Japanese-flagged mid-band satellite constellation
-
Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile to build disaster-resilient, uninterrupted communications infrastructure, strengthening economic security
for Japan
-
AST SpaceMobile to supply satellites to power Japan’s sovereign direct-to-device constellation
Tokyo
and Midland, Texas – November 9, 2026 – Rakuten Group, Inc. and AST SpaceMobile, Inc. (NASDAQ: ASTS), the company
building the first and only space-based cellular broadband network accessible directly by everyday smartphones, agreed to establish Rakuten
AST, Inc. on November 6, 2026 (Japan Standard Time)*1. The joint venture is tasked with building a direct-to-device communications
network in Japan using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to provide service to commercially available smartphones, strengthening Japan’s
communications infrastructure in the event of disasters and other emergencies.
The
Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications’ (MIC) selected the joint proposal from Rakuten’s preparatory company and
Rakuten Mobile, Inc. for the publicly solicited “J-LEO: Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project”*2.
Rakuten AST is expected to receive up to 148 billion yen (approx. 1 billion USD) in support over approximately three years under
J-LEO, through the Communications and Information Network Association of Japan (CIAJ), the organization established to manage the fund*3,4.
Through this joint venture, Rakuten AST will collaborate with AST SpaceMobile to deploy and manage satellites compatible with mid-band
spectrum, in order to establish a satellite communications network and commence domestic operations by the end of March 2029.
 | 
The
J-LEO Project will leverage the largest communication satellites ever deployed in LEO to build domestic communications infrastructure
that enables direct satellite-to-smartphone connectivity and strengthens economic security. In addition to extending cellular broadband
connectivity to areas with limited or no terrestrial coverage, the project aims to ensure cellular broadband connectivity during emergencies,
such as natural disasters, by establishing a framework for emergency inter-carrier roaming among mobile network operators.
Through
Rakuten AST, Rakuten and Rakuten Mobile aim to establish a non-terrestrial network (NTN) managed and operated in Japan. The companies
will deploy and operate a resilient, stable communications infrastructure capable of maintaining priority and stable connectivity, independent
of external conditions – even in times of emergency.
The
satellite communications service to be deployed by Rakuten AST will leverage AST SpaceMobile’s large-scale satellites to enable
high-speed internet connectivity — such as video streaming and social media — on off-the-shelf smartphones without the need
for specialized equipment*5. Because the base station equipment is installed on ground-based infrastructure, Japanese telecommunications
operators can flexibly and autonomously manage and operate the network.
AST
SpaceMobile will supply the satellites to power Japan’s sovereign D2D constellation. Beyond priority Japanese domestic market usage,
Rakuten AST also plans to work with AST SpaceMobile to provide these services through AST SpaceMobile to its customers worldwide, subject
to regulatory approval.
Rakuten
Mobile will also work with AST SpaceMobile to advance the use of AI edge computing and plans to develop AI-driven spectrum management
technology, exploring their application for higher-speed data communications and industry-specific solutions such as IoT. The company
aims to expand its solution offerings beyond telecommunications carriers to include connectivity-reliant industries, such as logistics,
infrastructure monitoring, construction, and agriculture.
Mickey
Mikitani, Chairman and CEO, Rakuten Group, commented, “This project is a key pillar of Rakuten Mobile’s network strategy.
By building an integrated framework spanning satellite procurement through operations and accelerating technological innovation, we will
contribute to the development of disaster-resilient communications infrastructure and the improvement of Japan’s communications
environment. We will maximize capital efficiency and pursue the expansion of business opportunities in the satellite communications sector.”
Abel
Avellan, Founder, Chairman and CEO, AST SpaceMobile, commented, “This represents a significant milestone for AST SpaceMobile
and validates the importance of space-based cellular broadband connectivity as countries around the world increasingly recognize the
technology as a critical complement to terrestrial wireless infrastructure to realize the goal of 100% broadband availability wherever
people work, live and travel. Through our technology, we will enhance the resilience of Japan’s communications infrastructure while
strengthening our global network by leveraging capacity that can also be utilized outside of Japan.”
 | 
In
addition to this project, Rakuten Mobile plans to begin commercial-environment testing of its satellite-to-mobile service within 2026,
under the strategic partnership between Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile established in March 2020*6.
Rakuten,
Rakuten Mobile, and AST SpaceMobile will continue working toward the early realization of D2D satellite communications, advancing the
development of resilient communications networks.

The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism 
 Governor Christopher J. Waller 
At the Bank of England Watchers Conference King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well.1 
My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term. 
The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy. 
At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening.2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings. 
If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does. 
Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace. 
The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance. 
While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low. 
These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking. 
This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged—it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market—there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable. 
The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy? 
The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier. 
I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure. 
So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications. 
One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post–World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent.3 
If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons. 
One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI. 
Another reason for low dynamism is that low firing may be a consequence of the huge surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023 related to the pandemic. Workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again, and that may be limiting job-switching. If this is a large factor, it may be temporary—workers are in their jobs for a median of three years before switching again, and we are nearing that threshold for the last of the pandemic job switchers.
